principle_name: Sales Is Simple: Connect, Diagnose, Solve
author: Mike Weinberg
chapter: Chapter 1 – Sales Simplified and a Dose of Blunt Truth
when_to_use: When overcomplicating the sales process or feeling overwhelmed by new methodologies—use this as a grounding principle to refocus on the fundamentals.
when_not_to_use: Not applicable—this is a foundational mindset principle for all selling situations.
principle: New business development is fundamentally simple: potential customers have needs, and salespeople represent businesses with solutions to those needs. The job is to connect with the right prospects, determine if your solution meets their needs, and do that more and better than anyone else. All the complexity, fear, and mythology around prospecting obscures this core truth. Sales success is not a result of tricks or elaborate methodologies—it is the result of sharp, disciplined execution of the basics, applied repeatedly against the right targets.
questions_to_ask: Am I overcomplicating this situation when the real answer is to pick up the phone and get in front of more prospects?
What is the simplest, most direct action I can take right now to move this opportunity or start a new one?
recommended_action: Return to fundamentals when stuck or overwhelmed. Select the right targets, build a compelling story, make proactive calls, conduct structured sales meetings, and repeat at high frequency. Complexity is often a form of avoidance.
motm_application: MOTM's BD team sometimes gets caught up in elaborate strategy when the answer is simpler: identify companies that look like existing successful MOTM clients, pick up the phone or send a direct message, secure a meeting, ask great questions, and tell the MOTM story compellingly. High activity against the right targets produces results.

principle_name: The New Sales Driver: Targets, Weapons, Execution
author: Mike Weinberg
chapter: Chapter 4 – A Simple Framework for Developing New Business
when_to_use: When diagnosing why a salesperson or team is failing to bring in new business, or when designing a new business development strategy from scratch.
when_not_to_use: Not directly applicable to a single customer interaction—this is a strategic framework for a new business initiative.
principle: Every failure to acquire new business can be traced to one of three causes: (1) poor target selection or lack of focus on selected targets; (2) weak sales weapons or inadequate proficiency using them; (3) insufficient planning or failure to execute the attack. This simple diagnostic framework—Select Targets → Create and Deploy Weapons → Plan and Execute the Attack—forms the New Sales Driver. Before blaming market conditions, the competition, or economic factors, evaluate where the failure sits in these three categories. Most sales teams struggle in more than one area simultaneously.
questions_to_ask: Have we selected the right target accounts and are we staying focused on that finite list?
Do we have a compelling, differentiated sales story and are we using it confidently?
Are we actually making enough proactive calls, meetings, and touches—or just talking about it?
recommended_action: When new business results are poor, audit all three components: review the target list for strategic alignment, evaluate the sales story for client-focus and differentiation, and measure actual prospecting activity versus plan. Fix the root cause rather than prescribing a generic solution.
motm_application: When MOTM's new business numbers are below target, use this framework to diagnose the cause. Is the target list well-defined and focused on companies that match successful MOTM client profiles? Is the MOTM sales story client-focused and differentiating? Are BD reps actually making enough proactive outreach? The answer is almost always one or more of these three areas.

principle_name: Target Lists Must Be Finite, Focused, Written, and Workable
author: Mike Weinberg
chapter: Chapter 5 – Selecting Targets: First for a Reason
when_to_use: When setting up a new business development plan, reviewing an existing target list, or when a salesperson lacks focus in their prospecting effort.
when_not_to_use: Not directly applicable to an in-progress sales call or negotiation—this is a strategic planning principle.
principle: Selecting target accounts is one of the few genuinely strategic decisions salespeople make. The target list must have four properties: (1) Finite—a defined, manageable number of accounts to pursue persistently, not a pile of directories; (2) Focused—concentrated on accounts with similar profiles where expertise and language can be developed; (3) Written—documented in an actual list that is used daily; (4) Workable—achievable to penetrate with the available weapons and time. Salespeople who abandon their list after one failed attempt, or who maintain no defined list at all, doom their new business effort to failure. Even the best talent will fail if energy is directed in the wrong direction.
questions_to_ask: Do we have a written, specific list of target accounts right now?
Does the profile of our targets closely match the profile of our best existing customers?
Are we working this same list consistently, or have we changed direction after early resistance?
Is the list small enough to give each account serious, repeated attention?
recommended_action: Create a written target account list of 20–50 accounts (scaled to the sales cycle and market size) that closely match the profile of existing successful customers. Commit to that list. Work it with multiple weapons over an extended period before abandoning any account. Review and refine the list quarterly, not monthly.
motm_application: MOTM BD reps should have a specific written list of 20–30 companies that match the MOTM ideal customer profile—mid-size manufacturers or distributors with a sales team of 5–20, facing execution gaps. Each rep should know every company on their list by principle_name and maintain persistent contact over 3–6 months before removing a target.

principle_name: Target Accounts That Look Like Your Best Customers
author: Mike Weinberg
chapter: Chapter 5 – Selecting Targets: First for a Reason
when_to_use: When identifying which new accounts to pursue—especially when the existing target list appears misaligned with results.
when_not_to_use: Not applicable in an active sales conversation—this is a strategic target identification principle.
principle: The fastest shortcut to identifying the right target accounts is to study your best existing customers and find more companies that look, smell, and feel like them. What industry are they in? What is their company size? What titles do their decision makers hold? What problems were they experiencing before they engaged you? Where are they located? Building a target list of companies with matching characteristics dramatically increases conversion rates because you already know how to serve them, speak their language, and tell their story. Focusing on a vertical market or specific account type also builds a reputation, which creates referrals and word of mouth within that niche.
questions_to_ask: Who are our three best existing customers, and what do they have in common?
Are the companies on our target list similar to our best customers in industry, size, and problem profile?
Have we studied what made our top customers decide to engage us, so we can find more like them?
recommended_action: Analyze 3–5 of your best customers. Identify common characteristics: company size, industry vertical, sales team structure, key challenges, decision-maker profile. Use those characteristics to filter and rank your target account list. Pursue accounts that most closely match the winning profile first.
motm_application: MOTM's best clients share common characteristics: they are growing companies in manufacturing, engineering, or distribution; they have 5–20 salespeople; they have experienced inconsistent sales results despite having a capable product; and their sales management is frustrated with unpredictability. MOTM should use this profile to filter and prioritize every target list.

principle_name: Get to Prospects Early—Before They're Already Shopping
author: Mike Weinberg
chapter: Chapter 2 / Chapter 5 – Late to the Party
when_to_use: When strategizing account entry or evaluating whether to respond to an unexpected RFP or inbound inquiry that was not generated by proactive prospecting.
when_not_to_use: Not applicable to existing customers or accounts where a relationship is already established.
principle: Being late to the party in new business development—showing up after a prospect is already shopping, evaluating alternatives, or has issued an RFP—dramatically reduces win rates. When prospects are already in shopping mode, their opinions are formed, their evaluation criteria are being defined by someone else's framework, and you are playing catch-up in someone else's game. The best position is to have built the relationship before a need arises, so that when the prospect is ready to act, you are already known, trusted, and potentially helping them define the criteria. Proactive targeting ensures you get in early. Reactive selling means you get in late and play defense.
questions_to_ask: Is this an opportunity we created proactively, or one we stumbled upon after it was already in motion?
Are we the first or among the first to have built a relationship at this account?
If we're late, can we reframe the opportunity or do we need to assess whether it's worth pursuing?
recommended_action: Work target accounts proactively before opportunities emerge. Build relationships, conduct discovery calls, and deliver value early—so that when a decision cycle begins, you are already the known preferred partner rather than a late bidder. Be skeptical of unexpected inbound RFPs you had no role in creating.
motm_application: MOTM BD reps should be wary of responding to requests from companies they haven't proactively cultivated. If a company approaches MOTM for a proposal without prior relationship development, there is a risk that a competitor already shaped the brief. The much stronger position is one where MOTM developed the relationship, surfaced the problem, and helped the prospect articulate what they need.

principle_name: The Sales Story Is Your Most Important Weapon
author: Mike Weinberg
chapter: Chapter 7 – Your Most Important Sales Weapon
when_to_use: Before any prospecting campaign, telephone outreach, first meeting, or proposal—the sales story must be built first. It is the foundation of every other sales weapon.
when_not_to_use: Not applicable as a standalone action—the story must be embedded in every other sales weapon.
principle: Of all the weapons in the new business arsenal, none is more important than the sales story. The story is used in some form in every interaction: emails, LinkedIn outreach, phone calls, voicemails, first meetings, presentations, and proposals. A compelling, client-focused, differentiating story is a prerequisite for new business success. Most companies and salespeople do not have an effective, consistent story—each person tells it differently and most versions are self-focused and boring. The inability to tell the story effectively is one of the top reasons salespeople fail to acquire new customers. A weak story drains confidence; a strong story creates it.
questions_to_ask: If I asked five different people at our company to describe what we do in two minutes, would they all say the same thing?
Does our current story focus on what we do, or on the problems we solve and results we achieve for clients?
Could I tell our story from memory in under two minutes in a way that compels a prospect to want to meet?
recommended_action: Invest significant time building a strong, consistent sales story before launching any new business campaign. The story must be client-focused, differentiated, and memorable. Make sure every BD rep can deliver it consistently. Test it against the 'So what?' filter before deploying it.
motm_application: MOTM must have a single, compelling, client-focused sales story that every BD rep can deliver consistently. It should immediately communicate the sales execution problems MOTM solves—not MOTM's process or credentials. Every MOTM contact, email, phone call, and meeting must be built on pieces of this story.

principle_name: Your Sales Story Is Not About You—Lead with Client Issues
author: Mike Weinberg
chapter: Chapter 7 / Chapter 8 – Your Sales Story Is Not About You
when_to_use: Whenever constructing or evaluating a sales story, pitch, email, or voicemail—always test whether it leads with the customer's issues rather than the seller's capabilities.
when_not_to_use: Never—this principle applies to every single outbound message and customer interaction.
principle: The most common and damaging sin in sales storytelling is self-focus. Prospects are not interested in what you do or how great your company is. They are only interested in what you can do for them. A story that leads with your offerings, your processes, your history, or your people will cause buyers to immediately mentally respond 'So what?'—and tune out. A story that leads with the problems you solve, the pains you remove, the results you achieve for clients, and the opportunities you help customers capture immediately grabs attention because it speaks to things already on the prospect's mind. Leading with client issues positions you as a problem solver rather than a vendor, and delays the buyer's reflex resistance to salespeople.
questions_to_ask: Does our pitch or story start with what we do, or with what the customer is experiencing?
Would a prospect reading our email or hearing our phone call immediately think 'that's relevant to me'?
Can I list 5–7 specific client problems we solve or results we achieve that would resonate with our target?
recommended_action: Rewrite every sales communication—emails, phone scripts, pitch decks, LinkedIn messages—to lead with 3–5 specific client issues, pains, or results before mentioning anything about your company or what you sell. Test every message against 'So what?' from the buyer's perspective. If it doesn't pass, rewrite it.
motm_application: MOTM must not lead with 'We provide outsourced sales support' or 'MOTM is a sales consulting firm.' Instead, lead with: 'Managing Directors of growing manufacturing companies look to MOTM when their sales team generates meetings but doesn't convert; when follow-up is inconsistent; when the pipeline is unpredictable; and when good products are being undersold.' That opening immediately resonates with the right prospect.

principle_name: The Three Building Blocks of a Compelling Sales Story
author: Mike Weinberg
when_to_use: When building, revising, or reviewing the sales story used in any sales weapon—phone calls, emails, presentations, proposals.
when_not_to_use: Not applicable to a specific customer conversation—this is a story construction principle.
principle: A compelling sales story must include three building blocks in this specific order: (1) Client Issues—the pains removed, problems solved, opportunities captured, and results achieved. This is the most important section and must come first because it is where the story's power resides. Prospects engage when they hear their own situation described. (2) Offerings—a brief, plain-language description of what you sell. This is the least compelling section and should be kept short. (3) Differentiators—a specific list of reasons why you are the best choice to address the client issues listed in section one. The order matters: issues first earns attention; offerings provide context; differentiators justify selection. Leading with offerings or differentiators is a weaker approach.
questions_to_ask: Does our story lead with at least 3–5 specific client issues before we describe what we sell?
Is the offerings section brief and clear, without overselling or embellishing?
Do our differentiators directly connect to the client issues we lead with?
recommended_action: Write a one-page Power Statement with: (1) a 1–2 sentence headline, (2) a transitional phrase followed by 4–7 client issue bullets using emotionally charged language, (3) a brief offerings description, and (4) 5+ specific differentiators. Use this document as the foundation for every sales weapon.
motm_application: MOTM's Power Statement should lead with client issues like: 'frustrated with inconsistent follow-up from the sales team,' 'unable to enter new OEM accounts despite having a competitive product,' 'pipeline is unpredictable and the forecast is unreliable.' The offerings section is brief: structured sales process, coaching, and BD execution. Differentiators: deep industrial B2B expertise, accountability through embedded execution, not just advice.

principle_name: The Proactive Phone Call Is Still the Most Effective Prospecting Weapon
author: Mike Weinberg
when_to_use: As the primary weapon for securing first meetings with target prospects—especially when email and social media outreach alone are not converting to appointments.
when_not_to_use: Not a replacement for face-to-face—the phone call's primary goal is to secure the meeting, not to sell.
principle: Despite widespread pessimism about phone prospecting, the proactive telephone call remains the most direct and effective weapon for securing face-to-face meetings with target prospects. Email, social media, and other tools are supplements to—not replacements for—the phone. The phone is avoided primarily because of mindset, not effectiveness. Salespeople who believe they are important professionals with a genuine solution calling on prospects who might benefit—and who approach the call with a calm, confident, conversational tone—consistently outperform those who are nervous, scripted, or apologetic. The objective of the call is singular: secure the meeting. Not qualify. Not sell. Get the meeting.
questions_to_ask: How many dedicated hours per week am I spending making proactive phone calls to target prospects?
Am I calling with confidence, believing I genuinely have something valuable to offer this prospect?
Is the objective of each call laser-focused on securing a meeting, rather than qualifying or selling over the phone?
recommended_action: Commit to dedicated time blocks for proactive calling. Approach each call believing you are an important business professional who might be able to help this prospect. Use a calm, natural tone—not a scripted performance. Have a mini power statement ready. The singular goal is to secure a meeting.
motm_application: MOTM BD reps should not rely solely on email and LinkedIn for prospecting. The phone remains the most direct route to a meeting with an MD or VP Sales. Prepare a 60-second telephone mini power statement focused on 2 client issues MOTM solves and one differentiator, and call your target list proactively during dedicated 90-minute time blocks.

principle_name: Telephone Mini Power Statement: Lead with Issues, Ask for the Meeting
author: Mike Weinberg
when_to_use: When making proactive phone calls to target prospects to secure an initial meeting.
when_not_to_use: Do not use a lengthy mini power statement mid-call or as a voicemail—keep the phone version brief. This is not for use in the actual sales call itself.
principle: The proactive phone call requires a carefully crafted structure: acknowledge you're interrupting without apologizing; position yourself with 'I head up [role/territory/function] for [Company]'; deliver a brief telephone mini power statement (2 client issues + optionally 1 differentiator from the full power statement); stop talking and let the prospect respond; then ask for the meeting. Ask three times if necessary. Prospects are conditioned to say no reflexively—it is often only on the third ask that they relent and invite you in. The three magic words to use when asking for the meeting: visit, fit, and value. Avoid sounding like you're reading a script—conversational delivery is essential.
recommended_action: Build a telephone mini power statement of 2 client issues (choose 1 unique/provocative and 1 broad/universal) and optionally 1 differentiator. Practice it until it sounds completely natural. After delivering it, stop and let the prospect react. Then ask for the meeting—and be prepared to ask three times. Use language like: 'I'd like to visit with you to see if we might be a fit to help you address some of these issues.'
motm_application: MOTM's telephone mini power statement: 'I head up business development for MOTM. Right now a number of Managing Directors in manufacturing are looking to us when their sales team isn't generating new OEM accounts consistently—despite having a competitive product. We're also helping companies whose pipeline is unpredictable and whose sales effort lacks structure. [Stop.] I'd love to visit with you for 30 minutes to see if we might be a fit to help.' Then ask for the meeting.

principle_name: Ask for the Meeting Three Times
author: Mike Weinberg
when_to_use: Every time a prospect says no to an initial meeting request during a proactive call.
when_not_to_use: Do not continue past three asks if the prospect is clearly hostile or the call has deteriorated. This technique is for the reflex 'no,' not genuine rejection.
principle: Prospects are programmed to say no to salespeople. The reflex resistance is automatic and has almost nothing to do with how good your call opening was or how relevant your solution might be. The first 'no' is usually not a real no—it is a conditioned response. Salespeople who hang up after the first refusal consistently underperform those who are willing to ask three times. It is typically on the third ask that the prospect relents. Use the three magic words—visit, fit, and value—in the third ask: 'I understand you're busy, but visit with me anyway. I promise you'll get value from the conversation, even if we don't end up being a fit to help you.' Conflict avoidance is the #1 reason salespeople cave on the first no.
recommended_action: After the first no, calmly acknowledge the objection ('I understand you're busy / already covered / not looking right now') and ask again differently. After the second no, deploy the three-word combination ask. After the third, accept the outcome gracefully and follow up with a value-adding email or try again another day.
motm_application: When an MD says 'we're managing our sales team ourselves' or 'we're fine right now,' MOTM reps should not immediately back off. Say: 'I understand—visit with me anyway for 30 minutes. I promise you'll take away at least two or three ideas, even if MOTM ends up not being a fit for you.' Many of MOTM's best clients required this persistence before the first meeting.

principle_name: Win with Voice Mail: Use It as a Campaign, Not a One-Off
author: Mike Weinberg
when_to_use: Every time you reach a prospect's voicemail during a proactive prospecting call.
when_not_to_use: Do not leave a voicemail that is longer than 30 seconds or that attempts to cover the full power statement.
principle: Prospects return approximately 75% of their calls to voicemail. Rather than viewing this as a failure, treat voicemail as a strategic weapon. Use each message as one touch in a multi-message campaign. Key principles: (1) Adopt a positive perspective—voicemail is a free opportunity to position yourself; (2) Prepare and expect it—do not improvise; (3) Leave a snippet of one client issue from your power statement; (4) Keep it short and intriguing; (5) Plan for multiple messages with variety—a different client issue or angle each time; (6) State that you'll call again; (7) Be human—use gentle humor or mild guilt-tripping in later messages. Prospects almost never return a first voicemail from a salesperson, so design a campaign of 3+ messages before expecting a callback.
recommended_action: Prepare 3 different voicemail scripts for the same prospect—each using a different client issue or angle from your power statement. Vary the message each time. End every voicemail by stating your number slowly and saying you'll call again. On the third message, use light humor or a genuine appeal to humanity to break through.
motm_application: MOTM BD reps should prepare a 3-message voicemail sequence for each target. Message 1: 'I help companies like yours when their sales team isn't consistently generating new OEM accounts.' Message 2: 'Companies where the pipeline is unpredictable and the monthly numbers are hard to forecast.' Message 3: 'I've now called three times which probably means I've earned a callback based on persistence alone—even if just to tell me it's not a fit right now.'

principle_name: Discovery Always Precedes Presentation
author: Mike Weinberg
when_to_use: Before every meeting, presentation, or proposal—always ensure sufficient discovery has been conducted before presenting any solution.
when_not_to_use: Never—this is an absolute sales law with no exceptions.
principle: The most fundamental law in new business selling is that discovery always precedes presentation. Presenting before fully understanding the customer's situation is sales malpractice. Pitchmen and product-pushers present before they understand. Consultative sales professionals gather information first, connect with the prospect, and then tailor their message to what they learned. A first meeting cannot be a presentation—ever. Even when prospects request a 'capabilities overview,' push back and insist on a discovery conversation first. A doctor who spends an hour talking about how great they are before examining the patient and then writes a prescription would be considered incompetent. The same standard applies to salespeople.
questions_to_ask: Have we done enough discovery at this account to know specifically why this prospect might need our solution?
Are we presenting because we have earned the right through discovery, or because the prospect asked us to?
Can I fill in slide 4 of the presentation—'Our Understanding of Your Situation'—with specific, accurate bullets from our discovery work?
recommended_action: Before every meeting and presentation, conduct a checklist: Do we know the prospect's key problems? Do we know who the decision makers are? Do we understand their evaluation criteria? If not, schedule a discovery meeting first—even if the prospect asked for a presentation. If forced to present without prior discovery, open with 15 minutes of structured discovery questions before showing any content.
motm_application: MOTM should never walk into a first meeting with a company's leadership team and immediately present MOTM's methodology. Start with: 'Before we show you how MOTM works, help us understand your situation. Tell us about the three biggest challenges your sales function is facing right now.' The presentation—tailored to what you heard—follows the discovery.

principle_name: It's Your Call—Plan It, Own It, Don't Default to the Buyer's Process
author: Mike Weinberg
chapter: Chapter 10 – Mentally Preparing for the Face-to-Face Sales Call
when_to_use: Before every face-to-face or virtual meeting with a prospect or customer—especially first meetings.
when_not_to_use: Not applicable to casual follow-up calls or administrative touchpoints.
principle: The initial face-to-face call is the pinnacle of new business development—everything leading up to it was done to get here. Because of the effort invested in securing the meeting, failing to plan it is inexcusable. Without a plan, the meeting defaults to the buyer's process. The buyer asks 'what do you have for me?' and the salesperson scrambles. The buyer peppers questions and the seller spends 30 minutes on defense without learning anything about the customer. Conversely, a seller who opens with a structured agenda, earns the buyer's consent to lead, and follows a logical progression controls the meeting professionally—and leaves a memorable impression. The seller must own the call. Bring a pad and pen. Leave the projector at home. Plan to ask, not to present.
questions_to_ask: Who am I meeting, what are their styles, and how should I adapt?
What is a 'win' for us walking out of this meeting?
What is my agenda, and how will I share it with the prospect to earn buy-in?
What probing questions have I prepared to uncover this prospect's pains and opportunities?
recommended_action: Before every first meeting: write down the names and roles of attendees, describe each person's probable behavioral style, define a specific win objective, and outline a call plan with phases. Share a brief agenda at the start of the meeting. Do not show up without a plan and hope the meeting goes well organically.
motm_application: Before every MOTM first meeting, the rep should know: Who is attending? What do they care about? What does a win look like today? What 5–7 questions will uncover their sales execution problems? What agenda will I share? The first meeting should never feel like a presentation—it should feel like a professional diagnostic conversation that ends with clear alignment and a specific next step.

principle_name: Structure of a Winning Sales Call: Eight Phases
author: Mike Weinberg
when_to_use: For every first meeting with a target prospect—this structure applies to the full arc of the sales call.
when_not_to_use: Not a rigid script—adapt to the natural flow of the conversation while ensuring all phases are covered.
principle: A winning first meeting follows eight phases: (1) Build rapport and identify the buyer's style—adjust pace, tone, and language accordingly; (2) Share your agenda and set up the call—earn buy-in for how the meeting will flow; (3) Clean up any outstanding issues from prior interactions; (4) Deliver the Power Statement—your 2-minute client-issues-led story; (5) Ask probing questions across four categories: personal, strategic/directional, specific issue-seeking, and sales process questions; (6) Sell—present your solution tailored specifically to what you learned; (7) Determine fit and seek out objections—proactively ask about concerns before the prospect leaves; (8) Define and schedule the next step—commit both parties to a specific, calendar-booked action.
questions_to_ask: What is the buyer's communication style, and how should I adapt?
Have I shared the agenda and gotten their agreement to the flow?
Am I asking enough questions across all four categories, or rushing to present?
Have I proactively asked about concerns and fit before the meeting ends?
What is the specific, scheduled next step we agreed to?
recommended_action: Before every first meeting, map out each of the eight phases. Know how much time you will spend in each. Ensure the discovery phase (phases 5 and 6) takes up the majority of the meeting. Never leave a first meeting without defining and scheduling the next step on the spot.
motm_application: MOTM's first meeting structure: brief rapport building → share the agenda → deliver the MOTM Power Statement → probe the prospect's situation (sales team performance, pipeline health, new account acquisition, follow-up discipline) → link MOTM's approach to the specific issues uncovered → confirm fit and surface objections → agree on next step (demo, proposal, follow-up meeting) and book it before leaving.

principle_name: Four Categories of Probing Questions
author: Mike Weinberg
when_to_use: During the discovery phase of any first or second meeting with a prospect.
when_not_to_use: Do not use all four categories indiscriminately—choose questions that are relevant to the context and persona.
principle: Effective discovery in a first meeting requires four categories of probing questions: (1) Personal questions—what matters to this person individually, their goals, how they're evaluated, what would make their life easier; (2) Strategic and directional questions—what's happening in their market, competitive pressures, corporate initiatives, cost or growth priorities; (3) Specific issue-seeking and opportunity-seeking questions—targeted probes in areas where your solution creates value, linked directly to the client issues in your power statement; (4) Sales process questions—who else cares about this issue (decision authority and influencers), timeline, budget, willingness to change, evaluation criteria, competitive alternatives. Deals go dark when sales process questions are skipped. Listen deeply, take notes, and when you find a problem—dig. Don't just move to the next question.
questions_to_ask: What are you personally trying to achieve in this role over the next 12 months?
What market or competitive pressures are most affecting your business right now?
Tell me about your current approach to [specific issue from power statement].
Along with yourself, who else really cares about this issue?
How committed are you to making a change?
Where will the money come from to fund this?
What criteria will you use to make your decision?
What other alternatives are on the table?
recommended_action: Before every first meeting, prepare 3–4 questions for each of the four categories. Focus the most time on issue-seeking questions in areas where your solution creates value. Do not skip sales process questions—they prevent deals from going dark later. Listen deeply and dig when you find pain.
motm_application: MOTM issue-seeking questions: 'How consistent is your sales team with follow-up after initial meetings?' 'What percentage of your pipeline converts from first meeting to proposal?' 'When you look at last year's new account acquisition, how does that compare to your target?' MOTM sales process questions: 'Who else in your leadership cares about this?' 'What would need to happen for you to make a decision to change your current approach?'

principle_name: When You Find Pain—Dig. Don't Move On.
author: Mike Weinberg
when_to_use: The moment a prospect reveals a problem, pain, dissatisfaction, or opportunity during discovery—shift from broad questioning into depth-seeking follow-up questions.
when_not_to_use: Do not dig so aggressively that the conversation becomes an interrogation—read the prospect's comfort level and maintain rapport throughout.
principle: When discovery questioning surfaces a problem, pain, or opportunity that your solution addresses, the instinct to quickly move to the next question must be resisted. The right move is to camp out on that issue. Pour salt in the wound. Ask follow-up questions to understand the depth, frequency, consequences, and cost of the problem. Ask what the prospect has already tried to solve it. Ask what happens if it goes unaddressed. The more fully you develop the problem—its implications, causes, and consequences—the stronger the case for your solution and the more compelling the eventual proposal. Rushing past pain points to cover more surface area is one of the most common discovery mistakes.
questions_to_ask: How long has this been a problem?
What have you tried to solve it, and why hasn't that worked?
What happens to your business if this isn't addressed in the next 6–12 months?
What does this cost you—in revenue, time, reputation, or competitive position?
How does this affect other parts of your business or team?
recommended_action: Build a mental rule: whenever a prospect expresses a pain, problem, or dissatisfaction that your solution can address, do not move to the next question. Instead, ask at least 2–3 follow-up questions to understand it more deeply. Only move on once you have a clear picture of the problem's severity and business impact.
motm_application: When an MD says 'our sales team generates meetings but doesn't close them,' don't immediately jump to explaining how MOTM's coaching solves this. Ask: 'How long has this been the pattern? What have you tried to address it? What is this conversion problem costing you in pipeline right now? If this continues for another year, what does that mean for your growth targets?' This develops the pain before positioning the solution.

principle_name: Define and Schedule the Next Step Before You Leave
author: Mike Weinberg
when_to_use: At the end of every sales meeting, without exception.
when_not_to_use: Never skip this step—even if the meeting went extremely well. A great meeting without a scheduled next step is still a failure.
principle: No matter how well a sales call goes, if it ends without a defined and scheduled next step, it has failed. The best presentation in history, followed by a standing ovation, followed by the salesperson leaving without booking the next meeting, is a lost opportunity. The final stage of every winning sales call is to define what comes next for both parties—then schedule it before leaving. Use the prompt: 'What do you suggest as an appropriate next step?' Let the prospect direct, then suggest mutual actions. Then book it. Open the calendar. Shake on it. Confirm it. A mutual commitment—'I'll do this, you do that'—is far stronger than a vague verbal promise.
questions_to_ask: What do you suggest as an appropriate next step?
Based on our conversation, how about if I do X, and you pull together Y—does that work?
Can we book a date now so that both sides have it on the calendar?
recommended_action: At the conclusion of every meeting, ask for the prospect's suggested next step. Agree on mutual commitments. Book the date before leaving the room—open your calendar immediately and confirm. Do not accept vague 'I'll be in touch' agreements. Every meeting must end with a booked next step.
motm_application: Every MOTM first meeting must end with a specific calendar-booked next step: 'Based on what you've shared, I'll prepare a brief diagnostic summary of how MOTM would approach your situation, and we'll schedule a 45-minute follow-up call on [specific date] to walk through it—does Thursday the 15th at 10am work?' Book it before leaving. Do not say 'I'll send something and we can find time.'

principle_name: Seek Out Objections Before Leaving—Don't Avoid Them
author: Mike Weinberg
when_to_use: Near the conclusion of every sales meeting, after presenting and before confirming next steps.
when_not_to_use: Do not open objection-seeking before you have delivered your full value case and checked for fit—do this in the appropriate sequence.
principle: The best time to discover objections, concerns, and obstacles is while you are still face-to-face with the prospect. Most salespeople avoid inviting objections for fear of bad news. This is backwards. A concern the prospect shares during the meeting can be addressed or worked around immediately. A concern the prospect keeps to themselves becomes the silent reason the deal goes dark or is lost after significant investment. Proactively ask: 'It looks like we might be a fit to help you—what do you think?' Then listen carefully. If something feels wrong, ask directly: 'I get the feeling you have concerns about going forward—what are you thinking? I'd rather hear it now than pretend it doesn't exist.'
questions_to_ask: Based on our conversation, it looks like we might be a fit to help you—what do you think?
Are there any concerns or obstacles on your end that we haven't discussed?
I get the feeling something might be holding you back—what's on your mind?
Who else might have concerns about moving forward that we should address?
recommended_action: Build this into every first meeting as a standard step before discussing next steps. Ask directly whether there is a fit. Invite the prospect to surface objections. If the answer is positive, confirm it and proceed to booking the next step. If concerns emerge, address them directly or plan how to work around them.
motm_application: Before MOTM closes a first meeting, ask: 'Based on what we've discussed, it looks like MOTM might be the right fit to help you build a more consistent sales process—what's your reaction?' If the MD hesitates, ask directly: 'I sense some hesitation—is there a concern about how this would work in your environment?' Better to hear it now than three weeks later when the deal goes cold.

principle_name: Buyer's Reflex Resistance: It's Not Your Fault, But It Is Your Problem
author: Mike Weinberg
chapter: Chapter 12 – Preventing the Buyer's Reflex Resistance to Salespeople
when_to_use: When designing any prospecting approach, phone script, email, or meeting structure—always consider the second objective of shaping how the prospect perceives you.
when_not_to_use: Not applicable to an in-progress customer interaction—this is a design and mindset principle.
principle: Every buyer has an automatic, almost instinctive negative reflex resistance to salespeople. This was not created by you, but it is your problem to manage. Buyers' collective experience with self-absorbed, verbose, manipulative, or time-wasting salespeople has created a default defense shield. Every sales interaction must therefore have two objectives: the primary objective (get the meeting, make the sale, advance the opportunity) and the secondary objective (shape how the prospect perceives you—as a professional, problem solver, and value creator, not as a typical vendor). Every aspect of how you communicate—your tone, language, pacing, self-focus versus prospect-focus, and the questions you ask—either confirms or counters the buyer's negative stereotype of salespeople.
questions_to_ask: Does my phone call, email, or meeting approach sound like a self-focused pitch or a genuine problem-solving inquiry?
Am I talking more than I'm asking and listening?
After this interaction, will the prospect see me as someone who understands and can help them, or as someone who wants something from them?
recommended_action: For every sales interaction, define two objectives: (1) what you want to achieve; (2) how you want the prospect to perceive you. Audit your approach—phone calls, emails, opening statements—against the second objective. Replace self-focused language with prospect-focused language. Demonstrate that you are there to understand and help, not to sell.
motm_application: MOTM BD reps should ask before every interaction: 'Will this email, call, or message make me look like a self-absorbed vendor or a knowledgeable partner who understands what this MD is dealing with?' Lead every interaction with the prospect's world, not MOTM's offering.

principle_name: No One Defaults to Prospecting—Time Blocking Is the Only Solution
author: Mike Weinberg
chapter: Chapter 14 – Planning and Executing the Attack
when_to_use: When designing a personal sales plan or coaching a salesperson on time management and new business activity consistency.
when_not_to_use: Not applicable to a specific customer interaction—this is an execution and discipline principle.
principle: No salesperson ever accidentally prospects. New business development never happens by default—there is always something more urgent, more comfortable, or more reactive pulling salespeople away from proactive selling. The only proven solution is time blocking: making hard, calendar-protected appointments with yourself for proactive prospecting activity. Time blocks should be 90 minutes to 3 hours each. During the block, email must be closed, the phone set to DND, and all attention focused exclusively on outbound prospecting. The block must be treated as sacred—as unmovable as a meeting with a top client. Two time blocks per week is a minimum for anyone with new business goals. Without time blocking, prospecting will never happen consistently enough to produce results.
questions_to_ask: Do I have prospecting time blocks scheduled on my calendar for every week this month?
When I look at my last 30 days, how many hours did I actually spend in proactive outbound prospecting mode?
What is my plan for protecting those time blocks from internal meetings, client service requests, and distractions?
recommended_action: Schedule 2–4 prospecting time blocks per week in your calendar—treat them as non-negotiable. Each block should be 90 minutes to 2 hours. Turn off email and distractions. Work your target list during each block: calls, LinkedIn messages, emails, referral outreach. Track activity and hold yourself accountable to the quantity.
motm_application: MOTM BD reps should block two dedicated 2-hour prospecting sessions per week—every week, regardless of their current pipeline status. A full pipeline today means nothing if no new outreach is happening. Time blocking is the only behavior that produces consistent new business over time.

principle_name: Sales Is a Numbers Game—The Math Works, Work the Math
author: Mike Weinberg
chapter: Chapter 14 – Planning and Executing the Attack
when_to_use: When a salesperson's pipeline is thin, when new business results are below target, or when designing a sales activity plan.
when_not_to_use: Activity quantity alone is not enough—quality of targeting, story, and call execution must also be strong for the math to work in your favor.
principle: The uncomfortable truth about new business development is that it is a numbers game. Most top-performing salespeople are the most active salespeople. The more prospects you engage from a strategically selected, finite, focused list, the more opportunities you will uncover. Every salesperson should know their personal sales math: how many proactive calls produce a meeting; how many meetings produce a proposal; how many proposals produce a deal. Working backwards from revenue goals, you can calculate the daily and weekly activity required to hit targets. Increasing activity levels—against the right targets, with the right weapons—will produce results. Reducing activity is always the wrong answer when pipeline is weak.
questions_to_ask: How many proactive calls or touches does it take me, on average, to get a first meeting?
How many first meetings convert to proposals?
How many proposals convert to deals?
Working backwards from my revenue goal, how many calls or meetings do I need per week?
recommended_action: Calculate your personal sales math based on historical data. Define the minimum weekly activity levels (calls, meetings, proposals) required to hit your revenue target. Track activity daily. If results are below target, increase activity—don't wait, complain, or find excuses.
motm_application: MOTM BD reps should know: how many companies they need to call to get a first meeting, how many first meetings convert to discovery conversations, and how many discovery conversations produce proposals. If MOTM's average sales cycle requires 8 touches to produce a meeting and 4 meetings to produce a proposal, work backwards from the revenue goal to determine the weekly call volume required.

principle_name: Babysitting Existing Accounts Is the Enemy of New Business
author: Mike Weinberg
when_to_use: When evaluating how a salesperson is spending their time, especially when new business results are low despite the rep appearing busy and relationship-focused.
when_not_to_use: This principle does not suggest neglecting existing clients—it challenges over-investment in service activities at the expense of prospecting.
principle: One of the most common and overlooked reasons salespeople fail at new business development is the seductive comfort of existing client relationships. It is always easier to talk to someone who already knows and likes you. Responding to existing client requests provides immediate validation and a sense of usefulness. But over-investing in account management at the expense of prospecting—babysitting existing accounts—is a guarantee of new business failure. Highly relational salespeople are particularly vulnerable to this pattern. They love being needed. The opportunity cost is severe: a salesperson spending 95% of their time on existing clients is functioning as a customer service rep, not a sales hunter. If your new business numbers are consistently below target, the first question to ask is how your time is actually being spent.
questions_to_ask: What percentage of my time last week was spent on existing client service versus proactive new business development?
Am I the person doing things at existing accounts that an account manager or customer service team should be handling?
Am I using existing client relationships as a comfortable excuse to avoid the discomfort of prospecting?
recommended_action: Conduct a weekly time audit. Calculate the split between reactive (existing account service) and proactive (new business prospecting) activity. Set a minimum threshold for proactive activity and protect it. Delegate or redirect existing account service activities to non-sales roles where possible.
motm_application: MOTM BD reps who are heavily focused on servicing existing MOTM clients are doing valuable account management work, but they are not doing new business development. Both must be tracked separately. If a rep is spending less than 30% of their time on proactive outreach to new targets, their new business performance will remain weak regardless of client satisfaction scores.

principle_name: Own Your Sales Process—Never Default to the Buyer's Process
author: Mike Weinberg
chapter: Chapter 2 / Chapter 10 – They Don't Own Their Sales Process
when_to_use: Any time a prospect attempts to direct the sales process in a way that puts the seller at a disadvantage—especially requests for premature presentations, proposals, or demos before discovery is complete.
when_not_to_use: Do not use this principle as an excuse to be inflexible or unresponsive to legitimate customer needs—it is about maintaining strategic process control, not ignoring the customer.
principle: Salespeople who don't have a clear mental map of the path to a sale end up defaulting to whatever process the buyer dictates. This is almost always a disadvantage. Buyers direct the process in ways that serve their interests—not yours. Premature proposal requests, capabilities overview meetings before discovery, and demo-without-discussion requests all put the seller in a reactive, commoditized position. The seller who owns the process controls the dialogue, builds credibility, and earns the right to present solutions in the most compelling context. Owning the process does not mean ignoring the customer—it means having the confidence and skill to redirect the conversation toward a path that produces the best outcome for both parties.
questions_to_ask: Is the prospect asking me to skip steps in my sales process that are critical to winning the business?
Am I agreeing to this request because it is genuinely in both parties' interests, or because I don't want the conflict of pushing back?
What would happen to my chances of winning if I pushed back and insisted on conducting discovery first?
recommended_action: Define your sales process: discovery → proposal/solution → commitment. Apply this structure to every opportunity. When a prospect tries to skip discovery ('just send me a proposal'), push back politely: 'To give you our best recommendation, we need to understand your situation more fully first—can we schedule 30 minutes this week?' Refuse premature proposals.
motm_application: When a prospect says 'just send us information about MOTM and we'll review it,' MOTM should push back: 'We'd love to—but the most useful thing for you would be a 30-minute conversation where we understand your current situation first. That way we can send something actually relevant to your challenges rather than a generic overview. Can we do that this week?' Owning the process leads to better discovery, better proposals, and higher close rates.

principle_name: Go After the Giant Competitor—Bigger Is Not Always Better
author: Mike Weinberg
when_to_use: When competing against larger, more established incumbents or market leaders at target accounts.
when_not_to_use: Do not use this as an excuse for reckless or poorly planned competitive attacks—strategy and preparation still matter.
principle: Too many salespeople develop a defeatist attitude when competing against dominant, established players. This mindset is wrong and expensive. Larger competitors are often slow, clumsy, inflexible, arrogant, and complacent. They win 70–80% of battles, but there are significant spoils available in the 20–30% where the smaller, more agile, more committed competitor wins. You are never competing against the entire organization of a giant—you are competing against their sales rep and a small team. Out-hustle them in discovery, out-differentiate them in your story, out-customize your solution, and outwork them in relationship building. A David vs. Goliath mindset that expects to win some and lose most—while celebrating every win—builds a stronger new business engine than one that assumes defeat before the fight begins.
questions_to_ask: What are the weaknesses of the incumbent supplier that I can legitimately exploit?
Where has the incumbent been slow, complacent, or unresponsive at this account?
How can I outwork and out-discover the competitor's rep on this specific opportunity?
What can I bring that a large, established supplier structurally cannot—speed, flexibility, access, customization?
recommended_action: When competing against a larger incumbent, do more discovery than they will, build deeper relationships at more levels in the account, and demonstrate agility and commitment that a larger player cannot match. Frame your difference as a strength, not a weakness. Make your size an advantage.
motm_application: MOTM often competes against larger, more established sales training and consulting firms. MOTM's advantage: deep industrial B2B specialization, embedded execution (not just advice), and senior personal attention rather than junior consultant teams. Lead with these differentiators explicitly. Prove commitment by doing more discovery and customization than any large firm would bother with.

principle_name: Get into Deals Early—Be Proactive Before Opportunities Form
author: Mike Weinberg
when_to_use: When building a proactive account penetration strategy for target accounts that have not yet formally identified a need or initiated a purchasing process.
when_not_to_use: Not applicable to reactive inbound opportunities where the prospect is already in a buying cycle.
principle: Top-performing sales hunters work their target accounts before concrete opportunities materialize. They build relationships, conduct discovery conversations, and deliver value to prospects who are not yet actively shopping. When a need eventually emerges, the proactive salesperson is already trusted, already inside the account, already helping shape the criteria. Reactive salespeople are too busy managing existing accounts to work their target list and end up finding opportunities only after competitors have already been involved. By then, they're playing catch-up in someone else's game. Get in early, turn over rocks, and unearth opportunities before competitors know they exist.
questions_to_ask: Am I in regular contact with my key target accounts even when there is no active opportunity?
Have I built relationships at multiple levels at my target accounts—not just with the gatekeeper?
Is there anything I can deliver as value to this prospect right now that would earn me credibility and early access?
recommended_action: For your top 10–15 target accounts, establish a cadence of proactive contact—quarterly calls, relevant insights, industry information, or brief visits—even without a specific opportunity in play. Build relationships early so that when a need emerges, you are the first person the prospect thinks of.
motm_application: MOTM BD reps should not wait for manufacturing companies to 'have a problem' before making contact. Send industry insights, invite prospects to a relevant webinar, share a case study relevant to their sector, or simply reach out to say 'I've been thinking about your situation.' Being known and trusted before a need arises means MOTM is the first call when the MD decides it's time to address their sales execution problems.

principle_name: Presenting Is Not Selling—A First Meeting Cannot Be a Presentation
author: Mike Weinberg
chapter: Chapter 13 – I Thought I Was Supposed to Make a Presentation
when_to_use: Any time a prospect requests a 'capabilities overview,' 'demo,' or 'presentation' as a first meeting—and any time you are tempted to lead a meeting with slides and content rather than questions.
when_not_to_use: Presentations have a valid role in the sales process—at the right time, after discovery is complete. This principle targets premature presenting, not all presenting.
principle: Presenting and selling are not synonyms. Presenting is only one part of selling. The most common mistake in new business development is conducting a presentation before completing discovery. Without understanding the prospect's situation, a presentation is necessarily generic—it cannot be customized, it cannot address the prospect's specific pain, and it positions you as a vendor delivering a pitch rather than a problem solver offering a solution. By sales law, a first meeting cannot be a presentation. Even when forced into a presentation format (RFP, pitch meeting, capabilities overview), convert the first portion into a discovery session by sharing your agenda and asking questions before showing any slides or content.
questions_to_ask: Why did you invite us in today?
What does success look like for you one year after implementing a solution like this?
What is the one thing you'd most like to get from our time together?
What is your experience with your current approach, and what would you change about it?
recommended_action: If asked to present, insist on a pre-meeting discovery conversation first. If that is not possible, open the presentation itself with 10–15 minutes of structured discovery questions using your agenda: 'In order for us to present the most relevant content, I'd like to take the first few minutes to understand your situation.' Only present content after you know what will resonate.
motm_application: When MOTM is invited to 'come in and present,' resist the urge to bring a full deck and show everything. Instead: 'In order to make the next hour truly valuable, we'd like to start by understanding what's driving this conversation.' Spend the first 15 minutes with structured questions. Then tailor the remaining time to what you learned. You will leave a far stronger impression than any competitor who just pitches.

principle_name: Team Selling: Use Every Available Resource to Win Business
author: Mike Weinberg
when_to_use: When facing a prospect who has a specific technical, executive, or relational need that the primary salesperson cannot fully address alone.
when_not_to_use: Do not involve additional people in calls without a plan for how each person will contribute—team selling must be orchestrated, not improvised.
principle: Top-performing hunters are masters at using all available resources to win business. Too many salespeople operate as lone rangers out of pride or insecurity. Bringing a CEO, technical expert, or senior executive to a high-value call demonstrates commitment, accelerates relationship building, and tailors the conversation to the right level. When you are getting nowhere with a technical buyer who dismisses you as 'just the sales person,' a subject matter expert from your team can create an immediate connection. Senior executives in the room also focus the conversation on business issues rather than transactional details—and they become personally invested in helping you close. The key is to always remain in control of the call structure and agenda, even when others from your company are present.
questions_to_ask: Who from my organization would strengthen credibility or connection at this specific account?
Is there a senior executive I can bring to elevate the level of conversation?
Do I have a technical expert who could connect with the buyer's engineering or technical team?
Have I briefed everyone on my team about their role in this call before we walk in?
recommended_action: For high-value target accounts, proactively invite relevant team members—executives, technical specialists, senior managers—to join key calls. Brief them on the call plan and their specific role. Remain in control of the call structure. After the meeting, debrief with the team and assign follow-up actions.
motm_application: When MOTM is trying to penetrate a strategic target account where the MD is skeptical, bring the MOTM senior leadership to the first meeting. The presence of MOTM's most senior person signals commitment and allows for a more strategic conversation. Prepare the senior person for their role: 'You're here to build executive-to-executive rapport and to validate our approach—I'll handle the structure of the call.'
